topics.title: Meet the story: Daudet, Alsace and a late morning

learn.hook: Imagine waking up to find that from tomorrow your school may not teach in your own language. That is the morning Franz walks into.
points: Author: Alphonse Daudet, a French novelist and short-story writer of the 19th century.
Background: the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71. Prussia, led by Bismarck, defeated France and took the border districts of Alsace and Lorraine.
Narrator: Franz, a young schoolboy in a village of Alsace, tells the story in the first person, looking back on that day.
Opening: Franz is late and dreads being questioned on participles, which he has not learnt at all.
Temptation: the warm bright day, birds chirping at the edge of the woods and Prussian soldiers drilling in the field behind the sawmill pull him outdoors, but he resists and hurries to school.

example.q: Why does Daudet open the story with Franz being late and unprepared?
steps: Franz's fear of the participle test shows how little he cares for French lessons.
This careless attitude sets up a strong contrast with his deep regret later.
So the opening prepares the reader for the change in Franz.
example.answer: It shows Franz as a careless boy at first, so that his later remorse over losing French lessons feels sharper.

learn.reallife: Many Indian students skip a regional-language class thinking it is 'easy marks later'. Franz learns, too late, that a language can be taken away.

learn.hook: Picture your noisy classroom gone silent like a Sunday, and your strictest teacher smiling at you. Something is very wrong.
points: At the town hall a crowd stands before the bulletin board; for two years all the bad news (lost battles, the draft, the commanding officer's orders) had come from there.
Usually school begins with a great bustle: desks banging, lessons repeated aloud in unison, the teacher's ruler rapping on the table. Franz had hoped to slip in unseen under that noise.
That day it is as quiet as a Sunday morning. Franz expects a scolding, but M. Hamel kindly tells him to go to his place.
M. Hamel is in his Sunday best: his beautiful green coat, frilled shirt and little black silk cap, all embroidered, worn only on inspection and prize days.
Village elders sit silently on the back benches: old Hauser with his old primer, the former mayor and the former postmaster.

example.q: List three things that were unusual at school that day.
steps: Recall the normal routine: noise, bustle, ruler on the table.
Compare: it was silent, M. Hamel was gentle, he wore his special clothes.
Add the villagers sitting on the back benches.
example.answer: The silence, M. Hamel's kindness and best clothes, and the village elders on the back benches.

learn.reallife: When something big happens, Indians crowd around notice boards, from exam results to railway charts. In Franz's village, the notice board brought news of war.

topics.title: The order from Berlin and Franz's regret

learn.hook: One line on a notice can change a whole people's future. M. Hamel reads it out in a trembling voice.
points: M. Hamel announces the order from Berlin: only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.
This is their last French lesson; the new master arrives the next day.
Franz is shocked that he can hardly write French. He regrets hunting birds' eggs and sliding on the Saar; his grammar and history books now feel like old friends.
When Franz fails to recite the participle rule, M. Hamel does not scold him. He says that Alsace's great trouble is putting off learning till tomorrow.
He blames everyone: parents sent children to work on farms or in mills for a little more money, and he himself sent pupils to water his flowers or gave a holiday when he wanted to go fishing.

example.q: How did the order from Berlin change Franz's feelings about his books?
steps: Before: the books were a nuisance and heavy to carry.
After the order: he could lose French lessons forever.
So the books suddenly felt like old friends he could not bear to give up.
example.answer: His once-boring grammar and history books became like old friends he could not give up.

learn.reallife: Families sometimes pull children out of school to help earn money, as M. Hamel says Alsatian parents did. Laws like the Right to Education Act in India try to stop exactly this loss.

quiz.explain: A is false: Franz was shocked and sad. R is true, since he once found the books a nuisance.
quiz.mistake: Assumes his old dislike stayed after the announcement

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Why did M. Hamel blame the parents AND himself? What had each of them done?'
teach.praise: Spot on! Parents chose money, M. Hamel gave holidays, and everyone kept saying 'tomorrow'.
teach.nudge: Tell me what the parents did and what M. Hamel himself did wrong.

learn.hook: Ever noticed you understand a lesson perfectly on the day you know it is the last revision? That is what happens to Franz.
points: M. Hamel calls French the most beautiful language in the world, the clearest and the most logical, and asks them to guard it.
His key idea: when a people are enslaved, holding on to their language is like holding the key to their prison.
Grammar, then writing and history follow. Franz understands everything. New copies saying 'France, Alsace' hang from the desks like little flags.
Pigeons coo on the roof, and Franz wonders whether they too will be made to sing in German.
At twelve the church clock strikes, the Angelus rings and Prussian trumpets sound. Too moved to speak, M. Hamel writes 'Vive La France!' on the board and dismisses the class.

example.q: Explain: 'as long as they hold fast to their language it is as if they had the key to their prison' (paraphrase).
steps: Prison here means being ruled by a conqueror.
Language keeps a people's identity, culture and unity alive.
So a people who keep their language can one day win back their freedom.
example.answer: Language preserves identity, and with it the hope and means to regain freedom; it is the key to escaping foreign rule.

learn.reallife: India's freedom struggle used songs, newspapers and slogans in many Indian languages to unite people. Language kept the idea of freedom alive, just as M. Hamel says.

topics.title: Characters, mother tongue and linguistic chauvinism

learn.hook: Some people learn the value of something only when it is snatched away. Every main character in this story does.
points: Franz: careless and playful at first; then remorseful, sensitive and suddenly eager to learn.
M. Hamel: strict but devoted teacher of forty years; patriotic and deeply emotional at the end.
Villagers: they come to the class full of regret for not learning their language when they had the chance.
Mother tongue: it carries a people's identity, memory and culture; losing it is losing a part of oneself.
Linguistic chauvinism: forcing one's language on others, or treating other languages as inferior. Here the conquerors impose German on Alsace and Lorraine.

example.q: Is the Prussian order an example of linguistic chauvinism? Give a reason.
steps: Define it: aggressive pride in one's language and imposing it on others.
The order bans French and forces German on a conquered people.
So it fits the definition exactly.
example.answer: Yes. The conquerors force German on Alsace and Lorraine and deny people their own language.

learn.reallife: India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. Respecting every language, rather than forcing one, keeps such a diverse nation together.

topics.title: Themes and craft: delay, patriotism, irony and symbols

learn.hook: 'Kal kare so aaj kar' (do tomorrow's work today) runs Kabir's famous doha. Daudet's whole story is a painful lesson in that line.
points: Procrastination: the habit of putting off learning till tomorrow; M. Hamel calls it the great trouble of Alsace.
Patriotism and loss: the pain of war appears in the bulletin board, the silent class and Hamel's breakdown.
First-person narration makes Franz's feelings direct and personal.
Irony: the 'last' lesson turns out to be the best lesson Franz ever had; he understands everything only when it is too late.
Symbols and pathos: the bulletin board (bad news), the pigeons (absurd imposition), 'Vive La France!' (undying patriotism), with vivid, moving description.

example.q: Explain the irony in the title 'The Last Lesson'.
steps: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what happens.
Franz never cared for lessons, yet the final one is the one he understands best.
The people value French only when it is about to be taken away.
example.answer: The last lesson becomes the most meaningful one; value is realised only at the moment of loss.

learn.reallife: Exam toppers often say, 'Start revision early.' Board students who delay till the last week feel exactly what Franz felt about French.

teach.nudge: Tell me what is surprising about the last lesson being the best.

topics.title: Words from the lesson and the past perfect

learn.hook: 'Tycoon' comes from Japan and 'robot' from Czech. English is a borrower, and this lesson asks you to trace its loans.
points: Phrases from the text: 'in great dread of' (very afraid of), 'counted on' (relied on), 'thumbing the pages' (turning pages with the thumb), 'a great bustle' (busy noise), 'reproach ourselves with' (blame ourselves for).
Word origins: tycoon (Japanese, 'great lord'), tulip (Turkish word for turban), logo (Greek 'logos', word), zero (Arabic 'sifr'), trek (Dutch/Afrikaans, to travel), robot (Czech), bandicoot (Telugu).
Choose a meaning from context: read the whole sentence and pick the sense that fits.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows the earlier of two past actions, e.g. 'I had counted on the noise to reach my desk unseen.'

example.q: Combine using the past perfect: Franz reached school. The lesson began before that.
steps: Identify the earlier action: the lesson began.
Put the earlier action in the past perfect: had begun.
Keep the later action in the simple past: reached.
example.answer: When Franz reached school, the lesson had already begun.

learn.reallife: Many English words come from Indian languages too: 'jungle', 'shampoo', 'bungalow', 'pyjamas'. Language borrowing shows how cultures meet.

I ___ on the bustle to get to my desk unseen.

quiz.q: 'In great dread of' means
quiz.explain: Dread is great fear; Franz feared being questioned.
quiz.mistake: Confuses dread with excitement

quiz.q: 'I had counted on the bustle' — 'counted on' means
quiz.explain: To count on is to depend or rely on something.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'count' literally as adding numbers

quiz.q: 'Thumbing the pages' of a primer means
options: tearing the pages out one by one
turning the pages with the thumb
quiz.explain: Old Hauser's primer was worn at the edges from turning its pages.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from 'thumb' without the action

quiz.q: The word 'tycoon' comes from
quiz.explain: It comes from Japanese 'taikun', meaning great lord.
quiz.mistake: Assumes an Asian word must be Chinese

quiz.q: The word 'zero' comes, through Italian, from
quiz.explain: Zero comes from Arabic 'sifr' through Italian; the concept of zero was developed in India, but the English word traces to Arabic.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the origin of the idea with the origin of the word

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect correctly?
options: The bell has rang before Franz arrived.
The bell had ring before Franz arrived.
The bell had rung before Franz arrived.
The bell was ring before Franz arrived.
quiz.explain: Past perfect is had + past participle: had rung; it shows the earlier action.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong verb form after 'had'

quiz.q: In 'we've all a great deal to reproach ourselves with', 'reproach' means
quiz.explain: To reproach is to criticise or blame someone, here oneself.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up reproach with approach

quiz.q: Choose the correct meaning of 'bustle' in 'the great bustle of the class'.
quiz.explain: Here bustle means the busy noise of desks and voices.
quiz.mistake: Picks another meaning of the word not fitting the context

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'When do I use had + past participle? Teach me with a Franz sentence!'
teach.praise: Hooray! Past perfect shows the earlier past action, like 'the lesson had begun when Franz arrived'.
teach.nudge: Tell me what the past perfect shows about two past actions.

topics.title: Board exam practice: The Last Lesson

learn.hook: Board examiners love this story. A sharp 40–50 word answer on M. Hamel or Franz can be your easiest marks.
points: Short answers (40–50 words): make one clear point, support it with one detail from the text, and end with its significance.
Common 'think as you read' questions: what Franz expected, what was unusual, what was on the bulletin board, what changed after the order, how Franz's feelings changed.
Long answers (120–150 words): for 'importance of mother tongue', use the key-to-the-prison idea, the villagers' regret and the theme of identity.
Discussion questions: peoples who lost their languages, problems of linguistic minorities, and whether pride in language can go too far (linguistic chauvinism).

example.q: Draft a 40–50 word answer: How did the people realise the value of their language?
steps: Point: they realised its value only when it was being taken away.
Evidence: villagers sat in the class; Franz regretted wasted time.
Significance: they understood language is their identity.
example.answer: When the order from Berlin banned French, villagers came to the last lesson full of regret and Franz wished he had studied. Losing French made them see that their language was their identity and the key to their freedom.

learn.reallife: Debates on mother-tongue education in India, as in the NEP 2020 emphasis on home language in early years, echo the questions this story raises.

games.title: Short or long answer topic?
items: What did Franz see on his way to school?
Why was M. Hamel in his Sunday clothes?
What was on the bulletin board?
Importance of the mother tongue, as shown in the story
How the story treats linguistic chauvinism and identity

games.title: Building a good short answer
items: Read the question and find its key word
State one direct point
Support it with a detail from the text
End with why it matters

quiz.q: What had Franz expected to happen when he reached school late?
quiz.explain: He feared a scolding and the ruler, which is why M. Hamel's kindness surprised him.
quiz.mistake: Ignores that he was late and unprepared

quiz.q: What was the main change the order from Berlin caused in the school?
options: French would no longer be taught
quiz.explain: German replaced French as the only language taught.
quiz.mistake: Invents a practical change

quiz.q: Which detail best supports the answer 'the villagers regretted not learning French'?
options: They stood reading the bulletin board
They drilled in the field by the sawmill
They sat on the back benches with primers
They rang the church bells at noon
quiz.explain: Their silent presence in class shows their regret and respect.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a detail that does not show regret

quiz.q: What do the pigeons' cooing and Franz's question about them suggest?
options: Pigeons can learn German quite easily
The school roof badly needed repair
Franz preferred birds to his teachers
Imposing a language is unnatural and absurd
quiz.explain: Franz imagines that even birds must change their song, which shows the absurdity of the order.
quiz.mistake: Reads the line literally

quiz.q: Which is the best opening line for a long answer on 'importance of mother tongue'?
options: A mother tongue carries a people's identity and freedom.
Franz was a lazy boy who liked to watch birds.
The story was first written in the French language.
Prussia had a very strong army in 1870.
quiz.explain: A long answer should begin with a clear thesis linked to the question.
quiz.mistake: Begins with plot detail instead of the main idea

quiz.q: A discussion question asks if pride in language can go too far. The term for this is
quiz.explain: Excessive pride that leads to imposing one's language is linguistic chauvinism.
quiz.mistake: Uses a term from another lesson

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Franz's feelings toward M. Hamel changed during the lesson.
Reason (R): He forgot all his past troubles with the teacher once he knew M. Hamel was leaving.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the thought of Hamel leaving made Franz forget the ruler and his crankiness, which explains the change.
quiz.mistake: Thinks R is an unrelated fact

quiz.q: Case: A student writes, 'M. Hamel was only strict.' What is missing from this character sketch?
options: His fear of the Prussian soldiers
His wish to give up teaching
quiz.explain: A balanced sketch adds that he was devoted, patriotic and gentle on the last day.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a one-sided description

teach.ask: Gappu needs exam help: 'Write me a quick answer: why did the villagers come to the class?'
teach.praise: A-plus answer! They came to honour M. Hamel's forty years and to show regret for not learning French.
teach.nudge: Add why they felt sorry and whom they came to honour.
